paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using information about the current situation, then learn from the resulting rewards. Linear reward models make these systems relatively interpretable and tractable, with strong guarantees when the model is correct. The paper addresses mobile health settings where assuming that rewards follow an unchanging linear relationship is difficult to justify.

The proposed model separates reward into a baseline component and a treatment effect. The baseline can have complex, nonlinear behavior, while the effect associated with treatment retains a simple form. This separation lets the model accommodate complicated background variation without demanding an equally complicated model of how an intervention changes the outcome.

The authors argue that this structure is plausible for mobile health and derive algorithms with strong performance guarantees comparable in character to those available for linear models. Experiments using data from a mobile health study support the theory. The contribution is a way to preserve useful simplicity in the treatment effect while allowing more flexibility in baseline rewards.
neurips-2017-action-centered-contextual-.tldr: Separating complex baseline rewards from simple treatment effects gives contextual bandits greater flexibility while retaining strong theoretical guarantees.

paragraphs: An autoencoder connects observed data with a latent code through an encoder and a decoder. This paper develops a variational autoencoder that treats the two directions symmetrically. One direction starts with observed data and encodes it; the other starts with a code sampled from a simple prior and decodes it into generated data.

Each direction defines a joint distribution over data and codes. The training objective seeks to bring these joint distributions together using a symmetric Kullback–Leibler divergence. At the same time, it seeks good marginal likelihoods for both observed data and latent codes, using learned lower bounds. Thus, matching the two routes and fitting their individual distributions become connected learning objectives.

The authors introduce an adversarial training procedure to support this formulation. Across several image benchmarks, they report state-of-the-art reconstruction and generation results. These findings support the usefulness of the symmetric objective for both recovering input images and producing new ones, rather than evaluating the model through only one of those capabilities.
neurips-2017-adversarial-symmetric-varia.tldr: A symmetric variational autoencoder uses adversarial training to align encoding and generation, with strong reported image reconstruction and generation results.

paragraphs: Statistics computed from interacting variables can fluctuate in ways that are harder to control than statistics of independent observations. This paper studies polynomial functions of the Ising model and asks how tightly their values concentrate. Such bounds help establish how much variation a statistic can exhibit under the model.

Under a high-temperature assumption, the authors prove concentration bounds that improve the guaranteed concentration radius by factors polynomial in the number of nodes. They also show that their results are optimal up to logarithmic factors in that number. The proof extends and strengthens an exchangeable-pairs approach, a technique for analyzing fluctuations through carefully related random quantities.

The paper connects these mathematical results to statistics for testing interaction strength in social networks. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate their usefulness in that role. The contribution combines sharper theoretical control of fluctuations with an application to network analysis; the high-temperature assumption is part of the stated scope of the concentration guarantees.
neurips-2017-concentration-of-multilinea.tldr: Under high temperature, sharper concentration bounds for Ising-model polynomials support statistics for testing interactions in social networks.

paragraphs: A predictor can be accurate yet too expensive to evaluate repeatedly. This paper studies classifiers and regressors whose prediction cost matters alongside their accuracy. Its starting point is that substantial savings are possible when most inputs require only inexpensive features and fast evaluations, provided those savings do not cause much loss in predictive quality.

The authors propose a budget-aware gradient boosting strategy based on deep regression trees. The method can grow very deep trees while keeping their average evaluation cost low. This distinction matters because tree depth alone does not determine the average expense of using the resulting predictor: a model can allow complicated decisions while keeping typical evaluations inexpensive.

Across several datasets, the authors report a large improvement over the state of the art considered in their evaluation. They also describe the method as easy to implement, with training time comparable to ordinary gradient boosting. The results suggest that accounting for prediction budgets during learning can produce practical savings without abandoning the flexibility of deep trees.
neurips-2017-cost-efficient-gradient-boo.tldr: Budget-aware gradient boosting learns deep trees that remain inexpensive on average, with strong reported performance and comparable training cost.

paragraphs: Representing a long paragraph as a latent code is useful only if that code preserves information needed by later tasks. The paper identifies a difficulty with recurrent neural network autoencoders: the quality of reconstructed sentences decreases as the text gets longer. This makes long passages a particularly demanding test of representation learning.

The authors propose a sequence-to-sequence autoencoder built entirely from convolutional and deconvolutional operations. It learns a representation by encoding text and reconstructing the sequence from that representation. They describe the framework as computationally efficient, simple to implement, and free of the length-related reconstruction issue motivating their work.

Experiments show better reconstruction and correction of long paragraphs than the recurrent models used for comparison. Evaluations on semi-supervised text classification and summarization also indicate potential for making better use of long unlabeled text. These downstream results matter because they test whether the learned representation is useful beyond reproducing its input, supporting the framework's proposed role as a component in language-processing systems.
neurips-2017-deconvolutional-paragraph-r.tldr: A convolutional and deconvolutional autoencoder improves long-paragraph reconstruction and shows promise for learning useful representations from unlabeled text.

paragraphs: An image can support several accurate descriptions, so a captioning system needs useful variation as well as correctness. This paper explores conditional variational autoencoders for that purpose. The authors identify a fixed Gaussian prior as a source of insufficient variation in the descriptions generated by standard versions of these models.

They propose two alternatives that organize the latent space around K components associated with different kinds of image content. Components can be combined to form priors for images containing several content types at once. One model uses a Gaussian mixture prior. The other introduces an Additive Gaussian prior, which combines component means linearly.

This construction gives the prior an explicit relationship to the mixture of content present in an image. In the reported comparisons, both models produce captions that are more varied and more accurate than a strong LSTM baseline and a standard conditional variational autoencoder with a fixed Gaussian prior. The Additive Gaussian version is especially promising, suggesting that compositional prior structure can improve both goals together.
neurips-2017-diverse-and-accurate-image-.tldr: Content-structured Gaussian priors help variational image-captioning models produce descriptions that are both more diverse and more accurate in reported comparisons.

paragraphs: Learning expressive neural network function classes is believed to be computationally difficult in the worst case. This paper asks what assumptions about the data can make efficient learning provable. It focuses on eigenvalue decay in a Gram matrix, a condition describing how quickly the magnitudes of the matrix's eigenvalues diminish.

The authors show that this distributional condition yields polynomial-time learning algorithms for expressive network classes, including feed-forward ReLU networks. Their results cover the non-realizable setting, where the labels need not be perfectly explained by a network in the class. They impose no assumptions on network structure or on the labels.

With sufficiently strong eigenvalue decay, the algorithms become fully polynomial in all relevant parameters for square loss. The strength of the decay therefore matters to the guarantee. The authors identify this as the first purely distributional condition giving polynomial-time algorithms for ReLU networks and note that eigenvalue decay has been observed on common datasets. That observation motivates the condition without making efficient learning unconditional.
neurips-2017-eigenvalue-decay-implies-po.tldr: Sufficient eigenvalue decay in the data's Gram matrix enables provably efficient learning of expressive neural network classes under square loss.

paragraphs: Online decision systems must choose actions while still learning which model best explains their observations. Thompson sampling addresses this by sampling from a posterior distribution over models. Although it has proved effective as a heuristic across many decision problems, directly computing and sampling from that posterior is tractable only in relatively simple cases.

This paper develops ensemble sampling as an approximation to Thompson sampling. The central aim is to retain a workable sampling-based decision procedure when the underlying models are complex, including neural networks. Using an ensemble provides an alternative basis for approximating the model uncertainty involved in Thompson sampling, making computational tractability a central design concern.

The authors establish theoretical support for the approach and provide computational results that add insight into its behavior. They present it as substantially broadening the range of applications where Thompson-style decision making is viable. The contribution concerns a tractable approximation with supporting analysis, so its significance lies in making the strategy usable with richer models rather than requiring exact posterior computation.
neurips-2017-ensemble-sampling-309278c20.tldr: Ensemble sampling approximates Thompson sampling to make uncertainty-driven online decisions tractable with complex models such as neural networks.

paragraphs: Semiparametric multi-index models combine a finite-dimensional component with a more flexible relationship between inputs and responses. This paper studies how to estimate the parametric component when the input dimension is high. Existing approaches can require covariates to be Gaussian or elliptically symmetric, restricting which input distributions their methods accommodate.

The proposed estimator uses a second-order Stein method with corrections based on score functions. These corrections provide a way to move beyond the Gaussianity and elliptical-symmetry requirements identified in earlier methods. The work also addresses heavy tails, which can make estimation difficult because unusually large observations can interfere with reliable statistical control.

The authors prove a near-optimal convergence rate even when the score function or response is heavy-tailed. To obtain the concentration results needed for that proof, they develop a data-driven truncation argument, which they suggest may have uses beyond this estimator. Simulations supplement the theory. Together, these results broaden the distributional settings addressed by high-dimensional multi-index estimation while retaining a strong statistical rate guarantee.
neurips-2017-estimating-high-dimensional.tldr: A score-corrected second-order Stein estimator achieves near-optimal rates for high-dimensional multi-index models beyond Gaussian covariates, including stated heavy-tailed settings.

paragraphs: Finding extreme weather in climate simulations requires more than assigning a label to an entire input: events also occupy particular locations and evolve over time. Available annotations can be incomplete, covering only some years or regions and missing events that are actually present. These gaps complicate fully supervised learning for the varied patterns researchers want to study.

The paper introduces a multichannel spatiotemporal convolutional network for semi-supervised bounding-box prediction and exploratory analysis. The approach uses both temporal information and unlabeled data. Bounding boxes address event localization, while examining learned representations provides another way to investigate the structure of the climate data.

The authors demonstrate improved localization from using time information and unlabeled examples. They also release the ExtremeWeather dataset to encourage further machine learning research on detecting and understanding extreme events. The contribution therefore combines a learning approach suited to incomplete annotations with a shared dataset, supporting research on climate patterns relevant to scientific understanding, risk management, and policy.
neurips-2017-extremeweather-a-large-scal.tldr: ExtremeWeather pairs a climate dataset with a semi-supervised spatiotemporal network that uses unlabeled data and temporal information to improve event localization.

paragraphs: Repeated measurements can follow a shared pattern over time while differing across individuals in both their values and their timing. This paper models such data when measurements lie in a Riemannian space. Its population trajectory is piecewise geodesic: it consists of connected path segments that respect the geometry of the measurement space.

The hierarchical mixed-effects model describes each subject through spatial and temporal transformations of that group-average path, applied component by component. This gives individual trajectories a common reference while allowing differences in their progression. Because the model is nonlinear, the authors estimate its parameters with the Stochastic Approximation Expectation-Maximization algorithm and validate that choice using synthetic data.

The application concerns monitoring chemotherapy in metastatic renal cancer. Using patients' RECIST scores, the authors estimate when patients escape from treatment and examine how different parameters relate to treatment response. The work provides a framework for representing shared and individual progression jointly, with the medical application illustrating how timing differences can become quantities of interest.
neurips-2017-learning-spatiotemporal-pie.tldr: A hierarchical geometric model learns shared progression and individual timing differences, with an application to chemotherapy response monitoring.

paragraphs: Scientific prediction often faces uncertainty about how the data were generated. That uncertainty can span a continuous family of possibilities, rather than two discrete training and testing domains. The paper seeks predictions whose distribution remains unaffected by nuisance parameters: unknown quantities that alter the data-generation process but are not the target of inference.

A quantity with this independence property is called a pivot. The authors introduce an adversarial-network training procedure intended to enforce that property on a predictive model and derive theoretical results for it. They also describe the same objective as fairness with respect to continuous attributes, connecting the statistical independence requirement to another interpretation of invariant predictions.

The method includes a hyperparameter for choosing a balance between predictive accuracy and robustness. This makes the competing objectives explicit instead of assuming that both improve together automatically. Demonstrations on a toy problem and particle-physics examples support the approach's effectiveness. Its central contribution is a training framework for controlling sensitivity to a continuous family of systematic uncertainties.
neurips-2017-learning-to-pivot-with-adve.tldr: Adversarial training encourages predictions to be independent of continuous nuisance parameters, with an adjustable accuracy–robustness trade-off.

paragraphs: Understanding a physical scene involves recovering an underlying world state from what appears in images and how it moves. This paper proposes learning that ability without human annotations. A perception module infers a physical representation, which physics and graphics engines then use to reconstruct the visual stream during training.

The authors call this process visual de-animation. At test time, the inferred world state becomes the basis for reasoning and future prediction through the generative models. Recovering inputs to a physics or graphics engine is computationally difficult, so the system uses a convolutional inversion network to recognize the state quickly from appearance and motion cues.

The framework can incorporate both differentiable and non-differentiable engines. Evaluations on synthetic and real datasets involving multiple physical scenes show good performance on state estimation and reasoning tasks. The authors also demonstrate transfer from synthetic training data to constrained real images. That qualification defines the reported transfer result, while the broader contribution is the integration of learned perception with explicit physical and graphical generation.
neurips-2017-learning-to-see-physics-via.tldr: Visual de-animation learns physical scene representations without human annotations by combining a perception network with physics and graphics engines.

paragraphs: Bayesian online learning updates a model after each new observation. For sum-product networks, these updates require moments of the model parameters under the posterior distribution. Earlier moment computation scaled quadratically with network size for general graphs, making repeated updates expensive, although tree-shaped networks already admitted linear scaling.

The paper gives an optimal linear-time algorithm for general directed acyclic sum-product networks. It first connects each edge's moment calculation to a joint inference problem. It then exploits the fact that the network represents a multilinear polynomial, using differentiation to evaluate the needed quantities without expanding a polynomial that may contain exponentially many terms.

A dynamic programming step shares computation across edges, reducing the total cost of all their moments from quadratic to linear. The authors use this result to construct a linear-time assumed density filter for sum-product networks. The practical significance is that efficient Bayesian updates no longer depend on restricting the network to a tree, broadening the structures for which online learning is computationally feasible.
neurips-2017-linear-time-computation-of-.tldr: Shared computation and polynomial differentiation make parameter-moment calculation linear in size even for general directed acyclic sum-product networks.

paragraphs: Model evidence, also called marginal likelihood, summarizes how a probabilistic model accounts for observations after integrating over its parameters. It is central to Bayesian model comparison and parameter estimation. Computing it can be difficult because the required sum or integral covers an enormous space of possible parameter values.

This paper studies evidence estimation through nonequilibrium simulation techniques connected to statistical physics. In probabilistic machine learning, related estimators are known as annealed importance sampling and reverse annealed importance sampling. The authors introduce estimators that combine forward and backward simulations, bringing information from both simulation directions into the evidence calculation.

Across several challenging models, the combined estimators outperform the forward and reverse approaches used for comparison. This is an empirical finding across the models studied, rather than a claim that one estimator must always dominate. The contribution is a way to use both simulation directions together for a difficult Bayesian computation, supported by comparisons showing advantages over using the existing directional estimators.
neurips-2017-model-evidence-from-nonequi.tldr: Combining forward and backward nonequilibrium simulations improves model-evidence estimation over forward and reverse AIS on the challenging models studied.

paragraphs: Optimal transport distances, including earth mover's distance, provide ways to compare distributions by the cost of moving mass between them. They are important in machine learning, statistics, and computer vision. The paper addresses a computational question left open by practical successes: whether general optimal transport distances can be approximated in near-linear time.

The authors establish that Sinkhorn distances achieve this goal through a new analysis of Sinkhorn iterations. The result gives a theoretical efficiency guarantee to an approach already associated with good empirical behavior. It concerns approximation of optimal transport distances, so the speed claim should be understood in that approximation setting.

The analysis also suggests Greenkhorn, a new greedy coordinate-descent algorithm with the same theoretical guarantees. Numerical simulations show that Greenkhorn substantially outperforms classical Sinkhorn in practice. The two contributions reinforce one another: the analysis establishes near-linear approximation, while the new algorithm turns that analysis into a method with an additional empirical advantage in the reported simulations.
neurips-2017-near-linear-time-approximat.tldr: A new Sinkhorn analysis proves near-linear optimal-transport approximation and yields Greenkhorn, which is substantially faster in reported simulations.

paragraphs: Generative and discriminative models take different routes to statistical learning, and their behavior can change when the number of parameters is large. This paper revisits their comparison for general exponential families in high-dimensional settings. Its focus is how estimation error converges, rather than declaring either modeling approach universally preferable.

The authors introduce a notion of separability for general loss functions and use it to build a framework for analyzing M-estimators, which estimate parameters by optimizing a data-based objective. The framework provides convergence rates in the infinity norm. This measures the largest coordinate error, making it useful for understanding whether any individual parameter remains poorly estimated.

They apply the machinery to obtain both infinity-norm and Euclidean-norm convergence rates for generative and discriminative models, revealing nuanced high-dimensional behavior. The results also cover differential parameter estimation, where the target is the difference between two generative parameter vectors. The contribution is therefore both a comparison of modeling approaches and a more general set of tools for studying estimation error.
neurips-2017-on-separability-of-loss-fun.tldr: A loss-separability framework yields high-dimensional convergence analyses for generative, discriminative, and differential parameter estimation.

paragraphs: Calcium imaging produces large streams of images that must be processed to recover neuronal activity. Methods that operate on large batches can struggle with the volume of recordings and delay access to results. This paper introduces OnACID to process incoming imaging data online, supporting analysis while an experiment is taking place.

The pipeline combines motion correction, neuronal source extraction, and activity denoising and deconvolution. These stages address movement in the images, identify the neuronal sources, and recover cleaner activity signals. The framework combines and extends earlier work in online dictionary learning and calcium-imaging analysis to discover and track hundreds of cells in real time.

The authors apply OnACID to two large experimental datasets, evaluate it against manually annotated data, and report that it outperforms a popular offline approach. Real-time processing also creates opportunities for closed-loop experiments, where ongoing measurements can inform experimental actions. The contribution is an automated streaming pipeline that connects the necessary processing stages closely enough to make that interaction possible.
neurips-2017-onacid-online-analysis-of-c.tldr: OnACID processes streaming calcium images to discover and track hundreds of neurons in real time, enabling closed-loop experimental workflows.

paragraphs: Recovering a sparse signal means finding a vector with relatively few nonzero entries from compressed measurements. Support recovery focuses specifically on identifying which entries are nonzero. This paper analyzes when computationally tractable hard-thresholding algorithms can achieve that goal, using the partial hard thresholding operator as a common framework.

Under appropriate conditions, the authors show that partial hard thresholding recovers an arbitrary s-sparse signal within O(s kappa log kappa) iterations, where kappa is a relevant condition number. The bound makes explicit how the required iterations depend on both sparsity and conditioning. Its guarantee is conditional on the recovery conditions used in the analysis.

By choosing particular versions of the operator, the authors obtain what they report as the best known results for hard thresholding pursuit and orthogonal matching pursuit with replacement. Simulated-data experiments complement the proofs and demonstrate effectiveness relative to other popular recovery methods. The main value is a shared analytical framework that explains support recovery across a family of algorithms.
neurips-2017-partial-hard-thresholding-t.tldr: Partial hard thresholding provides conditional support-recovery guarantees that unify and strengthen analyses of several sparse-recovery algorithms.

paragraphs: Compressing a collection of points is especially useful when the compressed representation still supports accurate distance estimates. This paper introduces a data-dependent representation with that goal. Starting from n points in d dimensions, each coordinate stored in B bits, it reduces storage while providing a mathematical guarantee on the recovered distances.

The representation uses O(d log(d B/epsilon) + log n) bits per point, compared with dB bits for the original coordinates. Distances can be approximated within a multiplicative factor of 1 + epsilon. This expresses an explicit accuracy–storage relationship. The authors report that their simpler algorithm nearly matches a recent theoretical bound.

They compare the method with Product Quantization on SIFT, MNIST, New York City taxi time series, and a synthetic one-dimensional dataset embedded in a higher-dimensional space. The resulting representations are comparable to or better than Product Quantization in those evaluations. The contribution brings practical compression performance together with a provable distance guarantee, connecting empirical usefulness to a clear mathematical preservation target.
neurips-2017-practical-data-dependent-me.tldr: A compact, data-dependent point representation preserves distances within a specified factor and compares favorably with Product Quantization in reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Linear inverse problems seek an unknown vector x from measurements y = Ax + w. The task becomes harder when parameters describing both x and the noise w are also unknown. This paper introduces Adaptive VAMP with auto-tuning, a simple iterative message-passing method that learns those parameters while estimating the vector.

The theory applies to right-rotationally random measurement matrices, a class that includes arbitrarily ill-conditioned matrices. This extends beyond the independent sub-Gaussian matrices required by earlier message-passing approaches. In a specified high-dimensional large-system limit, the algorithm gives asymptotically consistent parameter estimates under very general parameterizations.

The authors also show that each iteration's parameter estimates and mean squared error converge to deterministic values described by state-evolution equations. A testable additional condition ensures that the error matches the Bayes-optimal value predicted by the replica method. These qualifications matter: the guarantees concern the stated matrix class and asymptotic regime, with optimal error requiring the additional condition. Within that scope, the method offers both estimation guarantees and predictable dynamics.
neurips-2017-rigorous-dynamics-and-consi.tldr: Adaptive VAMP learns unknown distribution parameters and estimates signals with asymptotic guarantees for right-rotationally random matrices, including arbitrarily ill-conditioned ones.

paragraphs: A classifier need not answer every input. Selective classification allows it to reject some cases in exchange for lower error on those it accepts. This paper brings that approach to trained deep neural networks, giving users a way to specify a desired risk level and control the resulting reliability–coverage trade-off.

The proposed method constructs a selective classifier from an existing trained network. At test time, it rejects instances as needed to meet the chosen risk level with high probability. Coverage is the proportion of inputs for which it returns a prediction, so a stronger error requirement can come at the cost of answering fewer cases.

Experiments on CIFAR and ImageNet demonstrate the method's viability. The reported ImageNet example guarantees 2% top-5 classification error with 99.9% probability while retaining almost 60% test coverage. These figures describe error on the accepted predictions together with confidence in the guarantee. The result supports the possibility of using rejection to make deep classifiers more suitable for applications that demand controlled prediction risk.
neurips-2017-selective-classification-fo.tldr: A rejection mechanism lets trained neural networks meet a user-selected error target with high probability by reducing prediction coverage.

paragraphs: Showing that a neural network can represent a function does not by itself show that training can find it efficiently. This paper studies the standard stochastic gradient descent algorithm and proves a learning guarantee tied to the network's conjugate kernel space, a particular comparison class associated with the architecture.

For a rich family of architectures with logarithmic depth, SGD learns in polynomial time a function competitive with the best function in that kernel space. The benchmark is therefore a specified function class, rather than every function the network might represent. The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first polynomial-time guarantee for standard neural-network training at depths greater than two.

One consequence is efficient learning of constant-degree polynomials with polynomially bounded coefficients for depths from two through log(n). Another is that sufficiently large networks trained by SGD can learn any continuous function, although that result does not have a polynomial-time guarantee. Together, these statements connect representation capacity to learnability while keeping the efficient and unrestricted approximation claims distinct.
neurips-2017-sgd-learns-the-conjugate-ke.tldr: For a rich family of logarithmic-depth networks, standard SGD provably learns in polynomial time against the network's conjugate-kernel comparison class.

paragraphs: Neural language models with very large vocabularies must calculate probabilities over many possible words. This output computation can be expensive during inference. SVD-softmax targets fast, accurate probability estimates for the most likely words, where useful predictions need not require equally detailed computation for every vocabulary entry.

The method transforms the output weight matrix using singular value decomposition. For most words, it approximates probabilities using a few large singular values and their corresponding matrix elements. This allows the calculation to use only a small portion of the transformed matrix, reducing the arithmetic needed for a large-vocabulary output.

The authors apply the technique to language modeling and neural machine translation and provide guidance for obtaining a good approximation. For a vocabulary of 800,000 words, they report roughly 20% of the arithmetic operations and more than a threefold GPU speedup. These results demonstrate substantial inference savings in the reported setting, with the method specifically focused on accurately estimating the probabilities of the most likely words.
neurips-2017-svd-softmax-fast-softmax-ap.tldr: SVD-softmax reduces large-vocabulary inference work by approximating word probabilities from a small part of a decomposed output matrix.

paragraphs: Universal style transfer aims to apply arbitrary visual styles to content images. Fast feed-forward methods can struggle with styles they have not seen during training or sacrifice visual quality. This paper proposes an approach that handles a supplied style image without training on a predefined collection of styles.

The central mechanism is a pair of whitening and coloring transforms embedded in an image reconstruction network. Together, they directly match the covariance of the content features to that of the style features. Covariance describes how feature values vary together, giving the method a statistical target for transferring visual appearance. The authors relate this to Gram-matrix objectives used in neural style transfer.

The paper demonstrates high-quality stylized images through comparisons with several recent methods. It also examines whitened features and generates textures through feature coloring to investigate how the transforms behave. The contribution is a relatively simple feature transformation procedure that makes arbitrary-style transfer possible without learning each style as part of a predefined training set.
neurips-2017-universal-style-transfer-vi.tldr: Whitening and coloring transforms transfer arbitrary image styles by matching feature covariance without training on predefined styles.
